sources.airKgPerCubicMetre: Air at sea level in the International Standard Atmosphere, 15 °C
sources.referenceHeightMetres: The Beaufort scale, which our wind keeps, gives the wind at 10 m above the sea (WMO)
sources.gradientExponent: The wind over the open sea grows with height as (z/10 m)^0.11 (Hsu, Meindl & Gilhousen 1994, via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forces_on_sails)
sources.bluffDrag: A flat plate across the wind (NASA Glenn, Shape Effects on Drag, via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drag_coefficient): a hull's side and her furled rig, as the wind meets them
sources.crew: How fast her crew works her rig. walkMetresPerSecond: a person carrying the yard's heel along her, the normal walking speed of people on a rolling ship's deck, 1.28 to 1.68 m/s at the berth less 4 to 10% for the roll (Wang, Liu, Wang, Loughney, Yang and Gao 2020, Physica A 562, doi:10.1016/j.physa.2020.125369). haulMetresPerSecond: a line hauled or eased by hand, the rope-pulling speed at the lightest load measured, 1.87 m/s at 147.5 N (Arakawa et al. 2017, Sports Medicine International Open 1(4), doi:10.1055/s-0043-112335, a rope ergometer at maximal effort, the closest measured analogue): a sheet is worked with a turn round a beam (H&H 1:317), taking in what the sail gives, so the crew moves it at hand speed, not against its whole load
sources.camber: A full sail's depth over its chord: Marchaj's tunnel sails were cut to about 12% (AYRS 111, Rig Efficiency, Fig. 12)
sources.clothFriction: A cloth's friction drag over the dynamic pressure on its area, the share Masuyama, Nomoto et al. add to the pressure forces of a square sail to meet their tunnel's (MARSIM 2003): cloth carries pressure only normal to itself, and edge-on to the wind a sail keeps this alone
sources.sails: A sail is a thin wing of its own planform, from its rig's geometry: a crab claw a delta of its claw's angle, a square sail a rectangle as tall over as wide as the wind crosses it. While the flow holds to its lee side it presses normal to the cloth by the leading-edge suction analogy, C_N = K_p sin α cos α + K_v sin² α (Polhamus, NASA TN D-3767, 1966): K_p a delta's lift slope by Helmbold, K_v = (K_p − K_p²/πA)/cos Λ (eq. 13); a rectangle's K_p and its leading and side-edge vortex lift by Larson's fits (J. Aircraft 18, 1981) to Lamar's lattice (NASA TR R-428, 1974). Once the flow has left it, the cloth is a plate in the wind, pressed by the wind across it with bluffDrag, as her hull's side. Between breakdownDegrees and separatedDegrees the vortex bursts from the trailing edge to the apex, and the one gives way to the other. Measured where each planform's flow breaks: crabclaw a 77.5° sweep delta, as a 25° claw, its vortex bursting at the trailing edge at 37° and at the apex by 57° (Wentz and Kohlman, NASA CR-98737, 1969, Fig. 5.10.1, read off the plot); square a flat rectangle of aspect ratio 0.5, its normal force holding near its peak from 40° to 45°, easing to 51° and falling away at 52° (Winter, NACA TM 798, 1936, Fig. 3, read off the plot)
sources.clothKgPerSquareMetre: Experimental reconstructions of flax sails weigh 500 to 720 g/m² (Propylaeum, Heidelberg University, books.ub.uni-heidelberg.de/propylaeum/catalog/view/1035/1768/102856): a sail fills as the wind's pressure outweighs its cloth
